paper_name: Paper 1: Medicine in Britain, c1250–present and The British sector of the Western Front, 1914–18

questions.topic: Western Front: Blood Transfusions
questions.spec_topic: Context: Blood transfusions and developments in storage
questions.question_text: Outline two key characteristics of how blood transfusions were carried out on the Western Front (1914–18).
indicative_content: Blood was transferred directly from donor to patient using a syringe and tube (syringe-cannula technique) before storage methods were developed.
Sodium citrate was added to blood to prevent it clotting, meaning blood could be kept for several days before transfusion.
In 1917 at the Battle of Cambrai, Oswald Robertson established the first blood depot/blood bank storing blood in glass bottles with sodium citrate and glucose.
questions.examiner_tips: Candidates scored full marks by giving a specific feature and adding a separate sentence of supporting historical knowledge. Avoid vague statements like "it saved lives".

questions.topic: Western Front: Treatment of Battle Injuries
questions.spec_topic: The work of RAMC and FANY; medical care along chain of evacuation
questions.question_text: Assess the value of Sources A and B for an investigation into how frontline medical personnel treated combat wounds on the Western Front.
questions.stimulus: Source A: Testimony of volunteer nurse Shirley Millard working at a frontline Field Hospital (1918). Source B: Archival photograph showing a Casualty Clearing Station operating theatre (1917).
indicative_content: Source A gives useful evidence of rapid emergency surgery under extreme pressure and the emotional/physical toll on nurses.
Source B provides visual evidence of clean operating facilities, aseptic precautions (gowns, sterilised equipment), and artificial lighting in a CCS.

Provenance: Source A is an eye-witness diary from an American volunteer giving honest reflections; Source B is an official photograph taken by the Department of Information, possibly staged to reassure the home front.
questions.examiner_tips: Do not evaluate sources in isolation. Provide a sustained comparative judgement linking utility directly to the enquiry topic. Scrutinise origin and purpose, not just date.

questions.topic: Western Front: Treatment of Battle Injuries
questions.spec_topic: The work of RAMC and FANY; medical care along chain of evacuation
questions.question_text: Design a historical follow-up enquiry using Source A to investigate further how Western Front medical staff treated combat wounds.
indicative_content: Detail in Source A: Quote a specific detail about treatment, e.g. "We operated constantly without rest" or specific injury descriptions.
Question to ask: "What proportion of wounded soldiers survived emergency surgery at field hospitals?"
Type of source: Official medical logbooks or RAMC admission and discharge registers from that Casualty Clearing Station.
How it helps: It would provide statistical verification of survival rates to test whether the emergency conditions described in Source A were typical.
questions.examiner_tips: Ensure the enquiry question links directly to the quoted detail, and specify an authentic contemporary historical record (e.g. RAMC war diaries or hospital registers, not "the internet" or "a history book").

questions.topic: Medieval vs Industrial Hospital Care
questions.spec_topic: Approaches to prevention and treatment: hospitals across time
questions.question_text: Identify and explain one key difference between hospital care in medieval England (c1250–c1500) and hospital care in the industrial era (c1700–c1900).
indicative_content: Medieval hospitals were run by religious orders (monks and nuns) focusing on spiritual care, hospitality, rest, and prayer rather than medical treatment.

Industrial hospitals in the 18th/19th centuries were funded by charities and philanthropists, staffed by trained doctors and professional nurses (e.g. following Florence Nightingale’s reforms), aiming to cure diseases medically and surgically.
questions.examiner_tips: Write a single, tightly integrated paragraph comparing both eras directly using connective words ("whereas", "in contrast to"). Provide precise historical examples from both time periods.

questions.topic: Prevention of Illness c1700-present
questions.spec_topic: Approaches to prevention: smallpox vaccination, public health acts, modern government campaigns
questions.question_text: Analyse the reasons why methods of preventing disease advanced between c1700 and the present day.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Jenner’s 1796 smallpox vaccination
• Optional focus: compulsory measures in the 1875 Public Health Act
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Jenner’s cowpox vaccine proved immunity could be generated artificially, leading to government-mandated vaccination in 1853 and eradication of smallpox.
The 1875 Public Health Act marked the end of laissez-faire government attitude, compelling local councils to provide clean water, sewers, and refuse collection.

Own knowledge factor: Modern government health legislation and campaigns (e.g. clean air acts, compulsory childhood vaccinations, anti-smoking legislation, lifestyle advertising) targeting non-infectious conditions.
questions.examiner_tips: To reach Level 4 (10-12 marks), candidates must structure three distinct analytical PEEL paragraphs including at least one substantial factor of own knowledge beyond the stimulus points.

questions.topic: Understanding Cause of Disease c1250-c1700
questions.spec_topic: Ideas about the causes of disease and illness: Medieval to Renaissance
questions.question_text: ‘Understanding of what caused disease scarcely changed between c1250 and c1700.’ To what extent do you agree with this judgement?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: persistence of Humoral theory
• Optional focus: scientific inquiry at the Royal Society
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing: The Four Humours and miasma remained the dominant explanations during both the Black Death (1348) and the Great Plague (1665); supernatural and astrological beliefs persisted strongly.

Arguments disagreeing: The Renaissance brought humanism and empirical observation; the Royal Society (1660) promoted scientific testing; Thomas Sydenham classified diseases by symptoms; Leeuwenhoek observed animalcules (microbes) under early microscopes.

Sustained judgement: While the foundations of scientific enquiry shifted dramatically in the 17th century, ordinary people and doctors still lacked understanding of the actual cause (germs) until Pasteur in 1861.
questions.examiner_tips: Candidates must cover the entire date range (1250 to 1700). Evaluate both change and continuity before reaching a weighed, justified conclusion.

questions.topic: Advances in Surgery: 18th/19th Century vs 20th Century
questions.spec_topic: Advances in surgery: anaesthetics, antiseptics, high-tech surgery
questions.question_text: ‘Surgical breakthroughs achieved between c1700 and c1900 mattered more than surgical developments since c1900.’ To what extent do you agree with this view?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Lister’s antiseptic carbolic spray (1865)
• Optional focus: twentieth-century blood storage and transfusions
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Significance of c1700-c1900: Overcame pain (Simpson and chloroform 1847) and infection (Lister and carbolic acid 1865, leading to aseptic surgery), transforming surgery from a deadly last resort into a safe medical specialty.

Significance of c1900-present: Solved blood loss (Landsteiner blood groups 1901, sodium citrate storage 1914); enabled organ transplants (Barnard 1967); modern high-tech surgery (keyhole, microsurgery, robotic and laser surgery).
Sustained judgement: 19th century developments were foundational because without solving pain and infection, modern complex high-tech procedures would be impossible.
questions.examiner_tips: Avoid simply describing surgical techniques. Compare the relative significance and long-term consequences of breakthroughs across both eras.

questions.topic: Western Front: Trench Ill Health
questions.spec_topic: Ill health arising from the trench environment: trench foot, trench fever, shell shock
questions.question_text: Outline two key characteristics of soldier illnesses caused directly by trench conditions on the Western Front.
indicative_content: Trench foot was caused by standing in cold water and mud for long periods, causing numbness, swelling, and potentially gangrene requiring amputation.
Trench fever was caused by body lice in trench uniforms, producing severe flu-like symptoms, high fevers, and joint pains that put soldiers out of action for months.
Shell shock was caused by the psychological trauma of constant artillery bombardments, causing panic, tremors, nightmares, and mental breakdowns.
questions.examiner_tips: Ensure features relate specifically to the trench environment (e.g. trench foot, trench fever, shell shock) rather than direct battle wounds.

questions.topic: Western Front: Stretcher Bearers
questions.spec_topic: Transport and communications: stretcher bearers and evacuation chain
questions.question_text: Assess the value of Sources A and B for an investigation into the duties and challenges of RAMC stretcher bearers on the Western Front.
questions.stimulus: Source A: 1916 diary entry by stretcher bearer Private T. R. Green (8th Battalion KOYLI). Source B: 1917 photograph of bearers carrying a casualty through Third Ypres mud near Boesinghe.
indicative_content: Source A illustrates the physical exhaustion, constant danger from shelling, and psychological pressure experienced by stretcher-bearers during the Somme.
Source B shows the horrific terrain conditions of Third Ypres (Passchendaele), where four to six men were needed per stretcher due to knee-deep mud.
Provenance: Source A is private reflective testimony written near the time; Source B is an official photograph capturing authentic conditions, though possibly framed for home propaganda.
questions.examiner_tips: Link provenance directly to the enquiry. Consider why a stretcher-bearer’s personal diary offers unique insight into the emotional strain of the evacuation chain.

questions.topic: Western Front: Stretcher Bearers
questions.spec_topic: Transport and communications: stretcher bearers and evacuation chain
questions.question_text: Design a historical follow-up enquiry using Source A to investigate further the duties and challenges of Western Front stretcher bearers.
indicative_content: Detail in Source A: Quote a specific detail regarding casualty evacuation numbers or time taken.
Question to ask: "How long did it take on average to evacuate a wounded soldier from the frontline to the RAP?"
Type of source: Regimental Field Ambulance logbooks or RAMC War Diaries.
How it helps: Gives verifiable timeline data across multiple sectors.
questions.examiner_tips: Keep the enquiry question strictly focused on the quoted detail. Vague questions like "Was it dangerous?" will not receive credit.

questions.topic: Ideas About Causes of Illness: 18th/19th Century vs Modern
questions.spec_topic: Ideas about the cause of disease: Miasma/Spontaneous Generation vs Genetics/Lifestyle
questions.question_text: Identify and explain one key difference between beliefs about the causes of illness in c1700–c1850 and scientific explanations since c1900.
indicative_content: In c1700-c1850, people believed illness was caused by miasma (bad air from decaying matter) or spontaneous generation of microbes from rotting material.

In c1900-present, scientists know illness is caused by specific pathogenic microorganisms (bacteria, viruses), genetic abnormalities (DNA sequencing, Human Genome Project), and lifestyle factors (smoking, diet, alcohol).
questions.examiner_tips: Focus sharply on causes of illness rather than treatments. Explicitly compare both periods within one paragraph.

questions.topic: Renaissance Medical Knowledge c1500-c1700
questions.spec_topic: The Renaissance: Sydenham, Vesalius, Harvey, the printing press, Royal Society
questions.question_text: Analyse why medical knowledge and anatomical understanding advanced during the Medical Renaissance (c1500–c1700).
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: clinical observation by Thomas Sydenham
• Optional focus: wider circulation of texts via movable-type printing
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Thomas Sydenham advocated empirical bedside observation and classified diseases into species based on symptoms rather than individual humour balances.
The printing press (Gutenberg) allowed ideas and detailed anatomical diagrams (like Vesalius’s Fabrica) to be reproduced rapidly and cheaply without monk copy errors.
Own knowledge factor: Anatomical dissection breakthroughs by Vesalius (correcting Galen’s 300+ errors) and William Harvey’s discovery of the circulation of blood (1628).
questions.examiner_tips: Ensure your third paragraph draws upon specific Renaissance individuals (Vesalius, Harvey) or institutions (Royal Society 1660) with precise factual knowledge.

questions.topic: Galen & Medieval Medical Care c1250-c1500
questions.spec_topic: Medieval medicine: Galen, Four Humours, Church control, treatments
questions.question_text: ‘Medieval medical treatments failed primarily because practitioners relied uncritically on Galen’s writings.’ To what extent do you agree with this assessment?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: balancing humours via the Theory of Opposites
• Optional focus: Church-run medieval hospitals
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing: Galen’s incorrect theories (e.g. blood generated in the liver and consumed, Four Humours and Theory of Opposites) led to useless or harmful treatments like bleeding, purging, and dietary balancing.

Arguments disagreeing: Role of the Catholic Church in stifling enquiry (banning dissection, promoting Galen as dogma); lack of scientific technology (no microscopes); supernatural beliefs (astrology, sin, flagellation during the Black Death 1348).
Role of medieval hospitals: Focused on spiritual salvation and hospitality rather than medical care.
Judgement: Galen’s ideas were the framework, but Church enforcement and the lack of scientific instrumentation were the underlying causes of ineffectiveness.
questions.examiner_tips: Examine multiple factors (Church control, Galen’s ideas, lack of technology, supernatural beliefs) before reaching an evaluation of which was the "main" reason.

questions.topic: Role of Government in Medicine c1800-present
questions.spec_topic: Role of government: Public Health Acts, liberal welfare reforms, NHS 1948
questions.question_text: ‘Expanding public access to healthcare has been the single greatest change in state medical intervention since c1800.’ To what extent do you agree with this judgement?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: launching the National Health Service in 1948
• Optional focus: sanitary reform under the 1875 Public Health Act
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Significance of access to care/treatment: The NHS (1948, Aneurin Bevan) made healthcare free at the point of delivery for the first time, establishing universal access to doctors, hospitals, dentists, and ambulances.

Counter-arguments (Role in prevention/public health): The 1875 Public Health Act forced local authorities to provide clean water, sewers, and building regulations, defeating cholera and typhoid; clean air acts; compulsory vaccination acts (1853).
Modern lifestyle intervention: Anti-smoking legislation (banning smoking in public places 2007, plain packaging 2016), sugar taxes, and pandemic response.
Judgement: While public health prevention saved the greatest raw number of lives, the NHS fundamentally transformed everyday health and equality in Britain.
questions.examiner_tips: Directly compare the government’s role in providing treatment (NHS) against its role in prevention/public health (sewers, clean water, legislation).

questions.topic: Western Front: Thomas Splint
questions.spec_topic: Techniques for treatment: the Thomas splint
questions.question_text: Outline two key characteristics of how the Thomas splint was used to treat femur fractures on the Western Front.
indicative_content: The Thomas splint pulled the broken leg straight and held the bone rigid in traction, preventing the broken ends from grinding together and tearing femoral arteries.
It dramatically reduced the death rate from compound leg fractures from 80% in 1914-15 down to 20% by 1916-18.
questions.examiner_tips: State the mechanism (rigid metal frame pulling leg in traction) and the clinical outcome (reduction in compound fracture mortality from 80% to 20%).

questions.topic: Western Front: Gas Attacks
questions.spec_topic: The nature of wounds and injuries: gas attacks (chlorine, phosgene, mustard)
questions.question_text: Assess the value of Sources A and B for an investigation into the medical impact of poison gas attacks on the Western Front.
questions.stimulus: Source A: 1915 medical account by Captain J. C. Dunn (2nd Battalion Royal Welsh Fusiliers). Source B: John Singer Sargent’s 1919 war painting “Gassed”.
indicative_content: Source A provides immediate medical detail of physical symptoms: choking, coughing up green froth, lung damage, and blindness.
Source B depicts the scale of casualties, lines of blinded soldiers led to dressing stations, and the overwhelming demand on medical staff.
Provenance: Dunn was a frontline MO writing clinical observations; Sargent was an official war artist capturing the profound human impact of mustard gas.
questions.examiner_tips: Discuss the specific gas involved (chlorine/phosgene/mustard) and contextualise the development of gas masks from urine-soaked cotton pads to the Small Box Respirator (1916).

questions.topic: Western Front: Gas Attacks
questions.spec_topic: The nature of wounds and injuries: gas attacks
questions.question_text: Design a historical follow-up enquiry using Source A to investigate further the medical impact of poison gas attacks.
indicative_content: Detail in Source A: Quote a symptom, e.g. "men choking and coughing up green fluid".
Question: "How many soldiers exposed to gas required long-term hospital treatment or died?"
Type of source: RAMC casualty return records or Ministry of Pensions medical reports.
How it helps: Quantifies long-term disability and survival rates from gas attacks.
questions.examiner_tips: Ensure the source suggested is a specific contemporary record from military medical authorities.

questions.topic: Medieval Physician vs NHS Doctor
questions.spec_topic: Medical professionals across time: physicians, surgeons, apothecaries, GPs
questions.question_text: Identify and explain one key similarity between the work of a medieval university-trained physician and that of a modern NHS doctor.
indicative_content: In both periods, the primary role of the physician/doctor was to diagnose illness by examining the patient and identifying symptoms (e.g. medieval physicians examining urine color/pulse; modern doctors examining vital signs and prescribing treatments).
Both required extensive formal university education and recognised qualifications before being permitted to practice medicine.
questions.examiner_tips: Focus on similarity of professional function (diagnosis/prescription/formal training) rather than differences in medical understanding.

questions.topic: Science & Technology in Modern Medicine c1900-present
questions.spec_topic: Developments in science and technology: DNA, magic bullets, high-tech diagnosis
questions.question_text: Analyse why breakthroughs in science and medical technology accelerated medical progress from c1900 to the present.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: chemical magic bullets and chemotherapy
• Optional focus: Watson, Crick, Franklin, and Wilkins on DNA structure (1953)
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Chemical advances produced magic bullets (Ehrlich’s Salvarsan 606, Domagk’s Prontosil) and chemotherapy treating cancer by targeting specific cells without destroying the host body.
Watson, Crick, and Franklin’s discovery of the double helix structure of DNA (1953) and the Human Genome Project (completed 2003) enabled gene therapy and targeted treatments.
Own knowledge factor: Diagnostic imaging technology (X-rays, CT scans, MRI scans, ultrasound) and advanced surgical technology (electron microscopes, robotic laparoscopy).
questions.examiner_tips: Link each technological breakthrough directly to clinical medical progress (improved diagnosis, targeted cure, reduced surgical mortality).

questions.topic: Florence Nightingale & Hospital Care c1700-c1900
questions.spec_topic: Hospitals: changes in care and treatment, Nightingale, antiseptics
questions.question_text: ‘Florence Nightingale’s reforms contributed more than any other factor to improving hospital care between c1700 and c1900.’ To what extent do you agree with this view?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Nightingale’s Notes on Nursing (1859) and ward sanitation
• Optional focus: nineteenth-century anaesthetics in operating theatres
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Role of Nightingale: Reformed sanitation, ventilation, and cleanliness (reducing Scutari death rate from 42% to 2%); established professional nurse training (Nightingale School at St Thomas’ Hospital); published Notes on Nursing.

Other major hospital developments: Anaesthetics (ether, Simpson’s chloroform 1847) allowing complex internal surgery; Lister’s carbolic acid (1865) and antiseptic/aseptic hospital operating theatres; pavilion style hospital architecture; growth of specialist voluntary hospitals.
Judgement: Nightingale made hospitals clean places of recuperation, but without anaesthetics and antiseptics, hospitals could never have provided effective surgical treatment.
questions.examiner_tips: Distinguish between "care" (nursing, sanitation, environment) and "treatment" (surgery, anaesthetics, antiseptic medicine).

questions.topic: Infectious Diseases c1500-c1900
questions.spec_topic: Approaches to prevention and treatment: Great Plague, cholera, Jenner, Snow, Pasteur
questions.question_text: ‘Efforts to combat epidemic infectious diseases made minimal headway between c1500 and c1900.’ To what extent do you agree with this judgement?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: civic orders during the 1665 Great Plague
• Optional focus: John Snow’s 1854 Broad Street pump investigation
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing (continuity): During the Great Plague (1665), treatments (smoking tobacco, strapping chickens, bloodletting) were as ineffective as during the Black Death (1348); quarantine and isolation had limited impact; miasma still dominated until late 19th century.

Arguments disagreeing (major progress): Jenner’s smallpox vaccine (1796); John Snow’s Broad Street pump investigation (1854) proving cholera was waterborne; Pasteur’s Germ Theory (1861) and Koch’s bacteriology identifying specific pathogens; 1875 Public Health Act clean water infrastructure.
Judgement: Little improvement between 1500 and 1750, but radical transformation between 1850 and 1900 due to Snow, Pasteur, Koch, and public health legislation.
questions.examiner_tips: Break down the 400-year period chronologically, showing why the turning point occurred in the mid-19th century.

questions.topic: Western Front: Underground Hospital at Arras
questions.spec_topic: The context of the British sector: Arras, chalk tunnels, hospital system
questions.question_text: Outline two key characteristics of the Thompson Cave underground hospital at Arras (1917).
indicative_content: The hospital (Thompson’s Cave) was built inside vast underground chalk quarries and tunnels, making it completely protected from German artillery bombardment.
It was fully equipped with 700 beds, running water, electricity, and operating theatres, located extremely close to the frontline trenches.
questions.examiner_tips: Mention its safe underground chalk quarry location and its extensive medical infrastructure (700 beds, electricity, operating theatres).

questions.topic: Western Front: Trench Foot
questions.spec_topic: The nature of wounds and ill health: trench foot
questions.question_text: Assess the value of Sources A and B for an investigation into how trench foot affected soldiers and how the British Army responded.
questions.stimulus: Source A: British GHQ Routine Orders on foot care issued in 1915. Source B: First-hand recollection by Private A. West of the London Regiment (1916).
indicative_content: Source A reveals army preventive regulations: daily whale oil rubs, dry socks, buddy-system inspections, and officer discipline.
Source B shows the harsh frontline reality where soldiers neglected whale oil because boots were difficult to take off in freezing mud.
Provenance: Source A reflects official command strategy; Source B gives candid soldier testimony showing why official policy was hard to implement.
questions.examiner_tips: Highlight the contrast between official orders (Source A) and real frontline conditions (Source B) to judge practical utility.

questions.topic: Western Front: Trench Foot
questions.spec_topic: The nature of wounds and ill health: trench foot
questions.question_text: Design a historical follow-up enquiry using Source A to investigate further the problem and prevention of trench foot.
indicative_content: Detail in Source A: Quote regulation regarding whale oil rubbing or sock changing.
Question: "Did the routine orders of 1915 result in a measurable drop in trench foot hospital admissions?"
Type of source: Divisional medical inspection returns or RAMC casualty logs.
How it helps: Provides objective statistics on whether preventive orders worked.
questions.examiner_tips: Framing an effective follow-up question requires linking the quoted detail directly to an authentic statistical medical record.

questions.topic: Preventing Infectious Diseases: Renaissance vs Industrial
questions.spec_topic: Approaches to prevention: Renaissance quarantine vs 18th/19th century inoculation/vaccination
questions.question_text: Identify and explain one key similarity between measures used to curb infectious epidemics in c1500–c1700 and those used in c1700–c1900.
indicative_content: In both periods, local and national authorities used quarantine and isolation to stop diseases spreading (e.g. boarding up plague houses in 1665 with red crosses; isolating smallpox and cholera victims in isolation pest houses and fever hospitals in the 19th century).
In both periods, authorities took measures to clean streets and dispose of waste due to persistent beliefs in miasma (bad air).
questions.examiner_tips: Focus on continuity in government/local action (quarantine/isolation or street cleaning) across both centuries.

questions.topic: Attitudes Towards Surgery c1800-present
questions.spec_topic: Advances in surgery: anaesthetics, antiseptics, modern technology
questions.question_text: Analyse why public and professional attitudes towards surgical operations shifted between c1800 and the present day.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: pain relief via ether and chloroform anaesthetics
• Optional focus: modern keyhole, robotic, and microsurgical techniques
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Anaesthetics (Simpson’s chloroform 1847) transformed patient attitudes from sheer terror into confidence that surgery could be painless.
Antiseptics and aseptic surgery (Lister’s carbolic acid 1865, autoclaves, rubber gloves) reduced post-operative infection and gangrene, cutting mortality from 46% to under 15%.
High-tech surgery (keyhole surgery, robotic operations, organ transplants) made surgery minimally invasive with rapid recovery, making it routine and trusted.
questions.examiner_tips: Ensure the explanation links surgical breakthroughs directly to public and medical *attitudes* (confidence, trust, willingness to undergo surgery).

questions.topic: Medieval Care & Treatment: Role of Physician c1250-c1500
questions.spec_topic: Medieval healers: physicians, barber surgeons, apothecaries, women in the home
questions.question_text: ‘University-educated physicians played the central role in treating the sick in medieval England (c1250–c1500).’ To what extent do you agree with this view?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: scholastic university training based on ancient texts
• Optional focus: domestic and apothecary herbal remedies
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Role of physicians: Underwent 7-10 years of university training studying Hippocrates and Galen; possessed highest social status; diagnosed illness using urine charts, astrological calendars (zodiac man), and pulse.

Importance of other healers: Physicians were too expensive for ordinary people; barber-surgeons performed bloodletting and minor operations; apothecaries prepared herbal remedies; wise women and mothers in the home provided the vast majority of day-to-day healthcare.
Judgement: Physicians were prestigious for royalty and nobility, but for the general population, female family members and apothecaries were far more important.
questions.examiner_tips: Compare physicians directly against other medieval healers (apothecaries, barber-surgeons, wise women) across different social classes.

questions.topic: Pasteur & Causes of Illness c1800-present
questions.spec_topic: Ideas about causes of disease: Germ Theory, Koch, genetics, DNA
questions.question_text: ‘Louis Pasteur’s discoveries were the decisive turning point in explaining what causes illness from c1800 to the present.’ To what extent do you agree with this assessment?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Pasteur’s 1861 Germ Theory
• Optional focus: twentieth-century genetics and DNA research
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Pasteur’s Germ Theory (1861): Destroyed spontaneous generation; proved microscopic organisms caused decay and disease, providing the foundation for modern medicine.
Koch’s contribution: Isolated specific disease-causing microbes (anthrax, TB 1882, cholera 1883) using agar jelly and chemical dyes.
20th century genetics: Discovery of DNA structure (1953) and Human Genome Project (2003) explained genetic illnesses (cystic fibrosis, Huntington’s, cancer risks) which germs cannot explain.
Lifestyle understanding: Smoking causes lung cancer (Doll and Hill 1950), poor diet causes heart disease.
Judgement: Pasteur was the foundation for infectious diseases, but genetics revolutionised modern non-infectious pathology.
questions.examiner_tips: Balance Pasteur’s breakthrough in infectious disease against 20th-century discoveries in genetics and lifestyle.

questions.topic: Western Front: Transporting Wounded Soldiers
questions.spec_topic: Transport and communications: problems of terrain, stretcher bearers, horse vs motor ambulances
questions.question_text: Outline two key obstacles faced when evacuating wounded troops from Western Front battlefields.
indicative_content: The shell-cratered terrain, destroyed drainage, and deep mud (especially at Passchendaele) made it impossible for motor ambulances to reach the front, forcing reliance on stretcher-bearers.
Stretcher evacuation was slow and dangerous: carrying one wounded man required 4-8 stretcher-bearers under artillery and sniper fire, taking hours to reach the RAP.
questions.examiner_tips: State two distinct logistical problems (e.g. mud/terrain destroying vehicle access; enemy fire delaying stretcher teams).

questions.topic: Western Front: New Techniques to Deal with Injuries
questions.spec_topic: Techniques for treatment: wound excision/debridement, Carrel-Dakin method, Thomas splint
questions.question_text: Assess the value of Sources A and B for an investigation into innovative wound-treatment methods introduced on the Western Front.
questions.stimulus: Source A: 1916 medical journal report by surgeon Dr Alexis Carrel on antiseptic irrigation. Source B: 1917 official British photograph showing a Thomas splint applied to a casualty.
indicative_content: Source A explains the Carrel-Dakin antiseptic irrigation method for deep contaminated shrapnel wounds.
Source B provides clear visual proof of the Thomas splint keeping leg fractures aligned and immobilised.
Provenance: Carrel is a pioneer surgeon providing technical medical explanation; Source B is an official record demonstrating successful hospital treatment.
questions.examiner_tips: Evaluate how both sources illustrate the rapid evolution of surgical response to new industrial warfare wounds.

questions.topic: Western Front: New Techniques to Deal with Injuries
questions.spec_topic: Techniques for treatment: Carrel-Dakin method, Thomas splint
questions.question_text: Design a historical follow-up enquiry using Source A to investigate further innovative wound-treatment methods on the Western Front.
indicative_content: Detail in Source A: Quote Carrel’s method of flushing wound cavities with sodium hypochlorite solution.
Question: "What percentage of gangrene cases were prevented by using the Carrel-Dakin method compared to standard dressing?"
Type of source: RAMC surgical case registers from Base Hospitals.
How it helps: Provides objective clinical statistical evaluation of success.
questions.examiner_tips: Focus on clinical effectiveness and specific medical records (e.g. Base Hospital surgical logs).

questions.topic: Prevention of Illness: Medieval vs Modern
questions.spec_topic: Approaches to prevention: Medieval religious/miasma vs Modern vaccination/lifestyle
questions.question_text: Identify and explain one key similarity between medieval approaches to preventing illness (c1250–c1500) and modern preventative health since c1900.
indicative_content: In both periods, people believed that personal lifestyle choices and regime (regimen sanitatis in medieval times: moderate eating, exercise, bathing; modern healthy eating, exercise, avoiding smoking) prevented disease.
Both periods recognised the importance of avoiding foul environmental conditions (medieval carrying sweet herbs to avoid bad air; modern clean air legislation).
questions.examiner_tips: Highlight the conceptual similarity: personal responsibility for maintaining health through daily habits and diet.

questions.topic: Access to Medical Care & Treatment in Modern Period
questions.spec_topic: Role of government: Welfare reforms, creation of the NHS, development of GP practices
questions.question_text: Analyse why ordinary people gained far wider access to medical care and treatment in Britain from c1900 onwards.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: specialist NHS hospitals after 1948
• Optional focus: free family doctor (GP) consultations and Liberal reforms
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: The establishment of the NHS in 1948 made visits to hospitals and GPs free at the point of delivery, removing wealth as a barrier to healthcare.
GP practices were reorganised into local community health centres offering comprehensive primary care and preventive screenings.
Own knowledge factor: Liberal welfare reforms (1911 National Insurance Act providing sick pay and panel doctors for low-paid workers) and ambulance services.
questions.examiner_tips: Emphasise the removal of financial and geographical barriers to treatment.

questions.topic: Thomas Sydenham as Key Turning Point c1500-c1700
questions.spec_topic: The Renaissance: Thomas Sydenham, Vesalius, Harvey, Royal Society
questions.question_text: ‘Thomas Sydenham’s clinical methods marked the most important medical turning point of c1500–c1700.’ To what extent do you agree with this judgement?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: bedside observation in Observationes Medicae (1676)
• Optional focus: continued reliance on the Four Humours
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing: Known as the "English Hippocrates", Sydenham insisted on clinical bedside observation; classified diseases into distinct species; challenged the idea that each patient had a unique humour balance.

Counter-arguments (other turning points): Andreas Vesalius proved Galen made hundreds of anatomical errors by dissecting human bodies; William Harvey discovered blood circulation (1628), proving blood flows in a one-way system pumped by the heart; the Royal Society (1660) institutionalised experimental proof.
Judgement: Sydenham laid the groundwork for modern clinical diagnosis, but Vesalius and Harvey were equally pivotal in dismantling Galen.
questions.examiner_tips: Compare Sydenham against Vesalius and Harvey to evaluate which figure was the true "turning point".

questions.topic: Attitudes Towards Medicine c1700-c1900
questions.spec_topic: Industrial medicine: Jenner, Pasteur, Koch, Nightingale, Public Health
questions.question_text: ‘Public confidence in medical science grew steadily throughout the period c1700–c1900.’ To what extent do you agree with this statement?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: opposition and support surrounding smallpox vaccination
• Optional focus: breakthroughs against nineteenth-century infectious diseases
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing: Jenner’s smallpox vaccination proved diseases could be conquered; Pasteur’s Germ Theory and Koch’s bacteriology gave rational scientific explanations; anaesthetics (chloroform) removed the horror of surgery; Florence Nightingale transformed hospitals into clean healing institutions.

Counter-arguments (resistance and scepticism): Anti-Vaccination League opposed compulsory vaccination in the 1850s; early anaesthetics caused deaths ("Black Period of Surgery"); doctors resisted carbolic acid and handwashing initially (Semmelweis was ridiculed).
Judgement: Attitudes were initially sceptical and resistant, but by 1900, demonstrable reductions in mortality made public attitudes overwhelmingly positive.
questions.examiner_tips: Address both the growth of confidence and the significant public and professional resistance to new medical ideas.

questions.topic: Western Front: New Wound Treatment Techniques
questions.spec_topic: Techniques for treatment: wound excision/debridement, Carrel-Dakin method, Thomas splint
questions.question_text: Outline two key characteristics of new surgical or chemical techniques used to treat infected wounds on the Western Front.
indicative_content: Wound excision (debridement) involved cutting away all dead and infected tissue around a shrapnel wound to prevent gas gangrene before stitching.
The Carrel-Dakin method used a chemical antiseptic solution (sodium hypochlorite) pumped through rubber tubes to continuously irrigate deep, infected wounds.
questions.examiner_tips: Name specific surgical procedures (debridement or Carrel-Dakin) and describe how they functioned.

questions.topic: Western Front: Medical Staff in Casualty Clearing Stations
questions.spec_topic: The chain of evacuation: Casualty Clearing Stations (CCS)
questions.question_text: Assess the value of Sources A and B for an investigation into surgical and nursing care inside Western Front Casualty Clearing Stations (CCS).
questions.stimulus: Source A: 1916 wartime diary of military nurse Sister Edith Appleton at a CCS. Source B: 1917 official war sketch of surgeons operating inside a CCS during Passchendaele.
indicative_content: Source A illustrates the triage system, operating non-stop for 48 hours during offensives, and the physical/emotional resilience of nurses.
Source B depicts surgical conditions: multiple operating tables in large marquees, aseptic gowns, and artificial lighting under canvas.
Provenance: Appleton was an experienced QAIMNS sister recording authentic frontline impressions; Source B was commissioned to document wartime medical achievement.
questions.examiner_tips: Analyse the vital role of the CCS as the first place where life-saving surgery was performed on the Western Front.

questions.topic: Western Front: Medical Staff in Casualty Clearing Stations
questions.spec_topic: The chain of evacuation: Casualty Clearing Stations (CCS)
questions.question_text: Design a historical follow-up enquiry using Source A to investigate further the work of medical teams inside Casualty Clearing Stations.
indicative_content: Detail in Source A: Quote Appleton’s description of the triage categories (walking wounded, urgent surgery, moribund).
Question: "What proportion of casualties admitted to this CCS were operated on versus evacuated directly to Base Hospitals?"
Type of source: CCS admission registers and surgical logbooks.
How it helps: Provides factual breakdown of triage decision-making.
questions.examiner_tips: Tie the follow-up question to the triage system and cite contemporary CCS logbooks.

questions.topic: Treatment of Infectious Diseases: Medieval vs Modern
questions.spec_topic: Approaches to treatment: Medieval herbal/bloodletting vs Modern antibiotics/antivirals
questions.question_text: Identify and explain one key difference between treating infectious diseases in medieval England (c1250–c1500) and treating them in modern Britain (c1900–present).
indicative_content: Medieval treatments aimed to rebalance humours or appease God using ineffective methods like bloodletting, purging, herbal infusions, and prayer.
Modern treatments target specific pathogens directly using scientifically engineered pharmaceuticals such as antibiotics (penicillin) for bacteria and antivirals for viruses.
questions.examiner_tips: Contrast the theoretical basis: rebalancing invisible humours vs targeted chemical destruction of pathogens.

questions.topic: Why Little Change in Medieval Medicine c1250-c1500
questions.spec_topic: Medieval medicine: Church control, Galen, medical training, respect for tradition
questions.question_text: Analyse the factors that held back medical change in England throughout the Middle Ages (c1250–c1500).
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Church endorsement of Galen’s authority
• Optional focus: hospitality rather than cure in monastic infirmaries
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Galen’s theories (Four Humours, body designed by God) were adopted as dogma by the Catholic Church; questioning Galen was treated as heresy.
Monastery hospitals prioritised spiritual salvation, rest, and prayer rather than medical experimentation or curing physical illness.

Own knowledge factor: Education and training: Universities were controlled by the Church, teaching rote memorisation of ancient texts; dissection was forbidden or only used to illustrate Galen’s writings.
questions.examiner_tips: Focus heavily on the Catholic Church’s monopoly over universities, book production, and hospitals.

questions.topic: Progress in Medical Knowledge in Renaissance c1500-c1700
questions.spec_topic: The Renaissance: Vesalius, Harvey, Sydenham, Great Plague
questions.question_text: ‘Medical knowledge in England advanced substantially during the Renaissance era (c1500–c1700).’ To what extent do you agree with this view?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: William Harvey’s 1628 proof of blood circulation
• Optional focus: traditional responses to the 1665 Great Plague
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing (progress): William Harvey discovered circulation of blood (1628); Andreas Vesalius mapped human anatomy accurately; Thomas Sydenham classified diseases; the Royal Society (1660) championed empirical science.

Arguments disagreeing (continuity): Despite anatomical breakthroughs, understanding of disease causation remained unchanged (Four Humours and miasma still dominated); treatments during the Great Plague of 1665 were virtually identical to the Black Death of 1348; Harvey’s discovery had zero practical impact on medical treatments at the time.
Judgement: Enormous progress in scientific knowledge and anatomical theory, but almost zero progress in practical cures or clinical treatment for patients.
questions.examiner_tips: Crucial distinction: show the huge gap between *theoretical knowledge* (Vesalius, Harvey) and *practical treatments* (Great Plague 1665).

questions.topic: Role of Individuals in Prevention c1700-present
questions.spec_topic: Approaches to prevention: Jenner, Snow, government public health acts, lifestyle campaigns
questions.question_text: ‘Pioneering individuals mattered more than government action in preventing disease from c1700 to the present.’ To what extent do you agree with this assessment?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Edward Jenner’s smallpox vaccine
• Optional focus: modern state public-health and anti-smoking campaigns
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Role of individuals: Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine (smallpox 1796); John Snow discovered cholera was waterborne (1854); Louis Pasteur discovered Germ Theory (1861).

Role of government: Passed compulsory vaccination laws (1853); Public Health Acts (1848, 1875) funding sewers and clean water; public health education and anti-smoking legislation (banning tobacco advertising, smoking in public places 2007).
Role of science & technology: Electron microscopes, chemical synthesis of vaccines, genetic mapping.
Judgement: Individuals made key discoveries, but government legislation and funding were essential to turn those discoveries into nationwide disease prevention.
questions.examiner_tips: Weigh the importance of individual discovery against government implementation and technology.

questions.topic: Western Front: Nature of Fighting & Injuries
questions.spec_topic: The nature of the British sector: artillery, machine guns, shrapnel injuries
questions.question_text: Outline one key feature of Western Front weaponry or combat tactics that caused heavy casualty rates.
indicative_content: Artillery barrages: Explosive shells threw thousands of pieces of jagged hot shrapnel and dirt into the air, causing 58% of all battlefield wounds and catastrophic blast trauma.
questions.examiner_tips: State one feature clearly and add a specific explanatory sentence with historical detail (e.g. shrapnel causing 58% of wounds).

questions.topic: Western Front: Blood Transfusions
questions.spec_topic: Context: Blood transfusions and storage (Rous & Turner, Robertson)
questions.question_text: Outline one key feature of how blood transfusions were administered near the front line during the First World War.
indicative_content: In 1917, Oswald Robertson established the first blood depot at the Battle of Cambrai using sodium citrate and glucose to store blood in ice-cooled containers for up to 28 days before transfusion.
questions.examiner_tips: Award 1 mark for the feature (e.g. blood storage in depots) and 1 mark for supporting detail (Robertson / Cambrai / sodium citrate).

questions.topic: Western Front: Difficulties in Caring for the Wounded
questions.spec_topic: Evacuation chain: terrain, stretcher transport, overwhelmed dressing stations
questions.question_text: Assess the value of Sources A and B for an investigation into the practical difficulties of treating casualties on the Western Front.
questions.stimulus: Source A: 1917 RAMC medical officer diary describing waterlogged Third Ypres trenches. Source B: 1916 official photograph showing congestion outside a Somme Advanced Dressing Station.
indicative_content: Source A illustrates terrain difficulties: liquid mud, impassable shell holes, stretcher bearers taking 6-8 hours to carry one patient.
Source B depicts logistical congestion: dozens of stretcher cases lying in the open outside a dressing station waiting for transport.
Provenance: Source A is private testimony from an MO experiencing conditions firsthand; Source B is official photography verifying overcrowding.
questions.examiner_tips: Link utility to the enquiry question. Contrast the environmental barriers (Source A) with medical capacity limits (Source B).

questions.topic: Western Front: Difficulties in Caring for the Wounded
questions.spec_topic: Evacuation chain: stretcher transport, hospital capacity
questions.question_text: Design a historical follow-up enquiry using Source B to investigate further the practical difficulties of treating casualties on the Western Front.
indicative_content: Detail in Source B: Quote or describe the severe overcrowding of wounded soldiers waiting for treatment.
Question: "What was the average waiting time for urgent surgery during major Somme bombardments?"
Type of source: RAMC Field Ambulance and ADS daily duty logs.
How it helps: Provides objective time-to-treatment metrics.
questions.examiner_tips: Ensure follow-up enquiry focuses on the specific detail identified in Source B.

questions.topic: Epidemics: Great Plague (1665) vs Cholera (1854)
questions.spec_topic: Approaches to prevention and treatment: Great Plague vs Cholera in London
questions.question_text: Identify and explain one key similarity between responses to London’s 1665 Great Plague and responses to London’s 1854 cholera outbreak.
indicative_content: In both epidemics, people believed the disease was spread by miasma (poisonous bad air) and attempted to purify the air by burning barrels of tar or carrying pomanders.
In both epidemics, authorities attempted to isolate victims and clear refuse from streets, while wealthier citizens fled London leaving the poor behind.
questions.examiner_tips: Highlight the enduring belief in miasma causing both epidemics, or the similar public panic and flight of the wealthy.

questions.topic: Impact of Pasteur’s Germ Theory c1861-present
questions.spec_topic: Germ Theory: Pasteur, Koch, antiseptic surgery, vaccinations
questions.question_text: Analyse why Louis Pasteur’s 1861 Germ Theory transformed medical practice from c1861 to the present day.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Robert Koch isolating specific disease bacteria
• Optional focus: antiseptic and aseptic operating methods
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Koch applied Germ Theory to identify specific bacterial pathogens (anthrax 1876, TB 1882, cholera 1883), allowing medical science to target specific diseases.
Joseph Lister applied Germ Theory to surgery, using carbolic acid to kill bacteria on instruments, wounds, and hands, reducing surgical infection rates dramatically.
Own knowledge factor: Development of vaccines (Pasteur’s rabies vaccine 1885, modern MMR) and antibiotics (Ehrlich, Fleming, Florey and Chain).
questions.examiner_tips: Trace the causal chain from Pasteur’s microscopic proof to practical surgical, pharmacological, and preventive breakthroughs.

questions.topic: Four Humours & Medicine c1250-c1700
questions.spec_topic: Ideas about cause and treatment: Four Humours across Medieval and Renaissance
questions.question_text: ‘Between c1250 and c1700, diagnosis and treatment remained overwhelmingly dominated by the Theory of the Four Humours.’ To what extent do you agree with this judgement?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Galenic humoral balance
• Optional focus: herbal remedies, spices, and new New World ingredients
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing: The Four Humours remained the core medical model taught in universities for over 400 years; bloodletting, purging, and herbal diets were prescribed throughout both the Black Death (1348) and Great Plague (1665).

Arguments disagreeing: Religious explanations (punishment from God, sin) and astrology were equally dominant in the medieval period; in the Renaissance, Paracelsus introduced chemical remedies, Vesalius proved Galen’s anatomy wrong, and Sydenham insisted on classifying diseases by symptoms rather than humours.
Judgement: While humours underpinned everyday treatment, religious beliefs dominated the early period and scientific empirical observation was beginning to replace it by 1700.
questions.examiner_tips: Address the full 450-year span, contrasting medieval religious/humoral beliefs with Renaissance chemical and empirical developments.

questions.topic: Role of Government in Hospital Care c1800-present
questions.spec_topic: Hospitals and government: Nightingale, voluntary hospitals, NHS 1948
questions.question_text: ‘State intervention was the primary driver behind improved hospital care and treatment from c1800 to the present.’ To what extent do you agree with this view?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: founding the NHS in 1948
• Optional focus: nursing and ward hygiene after Nightingale (1859)
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Role of government: Nationalised hospitals under the NHS in 1948; invested in modern regional hospital architecture, specialist trauma units, and equipment; set national hygiene and clinical standards.

Role of individuals: Florence Nightingale transformed sanitation, ward design, and professional nursing standards without initial government direction; Joseph Lister invented antiseptic surgery; James Simpson introduced chloroform anaesthesia.
Role of science & technology: X-rays, MRI scanners, blood transfusion storage, penicillin, and high-tech robotic surgery transformed clinical capability.

Judgement: Individual innovators and scientific breakthroughs created modern hospital treatment, but government funding and organisation via the NHS was essential to make that treatment universally accessible.
questions.examiner_tips: Compare government intervention against individual reformers (Nightingale, Lister) and scientific technology.
